about: Sourced life stories for the Herods: the six rulers of the family and the women Scripture names with them, Herodias and Bernice. Written from Scripture and the reviewed dossier Research/People/rulers-herods.md.

herod-mat-2-1.short: The king when Jesus was born in Bethlehem; he questioned the wise men about the star and had the young children of Bethlehem killed.

paragraphs.text: Matthew calls him "Herod the king" and Luke "Herod, the king of Judaea". Scripture never calls him Herod the Great; that name, and the reasons for taking the Herod of Luke 1:5 as this man, are explained on his page as a ruler. Matthew gives the only family link Scripture states for him: Archelaus reigned in Judaea "in the room of his father Herod". Luke sets the angel's promise to the priest Zacharias of a son, John, "in the days of Herod, the king of Judaea".

Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea "in the days of Herod the king". Wise men came from the east to Jerusalem asking, "Where is he that is born King of the Jews?" When Herod heard it, "he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him." He gathered the chief priests and scribes and asked them where Christ should be born, and they answered, "In Bethlehem of Judaea", quoting the prophet.

Herod called the wise men privately and "enquired of them diligently what time the star appeared". He sent them to Bethlehem and said, "bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also." They found the young child with Mary his mother and worshipped him. Then, "being warned of God in a dream that they should not return to Herod", they went home another way.

An angel told Joseph in a dream to take the child and his mother into Egypt, "for Herod will seek the young child to destroy him". When Herod saw "that he was mocked of the wise men", he "was exceeding wroth". He sent and "slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under", reckoning by the time he had enquired of the wise men. Matthew does not say how many died; he sets beside it the words of Jeremy the prophet, "Rachel weeping for her children".

The family stayed in Egypt "until the death of Herod". Of his death Matthew says only, "But when Herod was dead"; then an angel told Joseph to go back, "for they are dead which sought the young child's life." Scripture does not say how Herod died or where he was buried. Hearing that Archelaus now reigned in Judaea, Joseph turned aside into Galilee and settled in Nazareth.

Acts tells that Paul, brought to Caesarea, was kept "in Herod's judgment hall". Acts does not say which Herod it was named for; the site files the verse under this man, as his page as a ruler explains.

archelaus-mat-2-22.short: A son of Herod, named once in Scripture: Joseph heard that Archelaus reigned in Judaea, was afraid to go there, and settled in Nazareth instead.

paragraphs.text: Archelaus is named in a single verse of Scripture. When Joseph came back from Egypt with the young child and his mother, "he heard that Archelaus did reign in Judaea in the room of his father Herod, he was afraid to go thither". Warned of God in a dream, he turned aside into Galilee and came to live in "a city called Nazareth".

That is all Scripture says of him. It records nothing he did or said, does not call him king, and does not tell how his rule ended. What else is known of him comes from outside the Bible and is set out, with its sources, on his page as a ruler.

herod-mat-14-1.short: Herod the tetrarch of Galilee, who married his brother Philip's wife Herodias, beheaded John the Baptist, and questioned and mocked Jesus before sending him back to Pilate.

paragraphs.text: The Gospels call him "Herod the tetrarch", and Mark once "king Herod". Luke names him tetrarch of Galilee in the year the word of God came to John in the wilderness, with "his brother Philip" tetrarch of Ituraea. Scripture never calls him Antipas; that name, and which verses the site gives to him, are explained on his page as a ruler. Manaen, one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, "had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch".

Herod had married Herodias, "his brother Philip's wife". Mark says John the Baptist told him, "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife." Luke says John reproved him for Herodias "and for all the evils which Herod had done", and that Herod "shut up John in prison". Matthew says Herod would have put John to death, but "he feared the multitude, because they counted him as a prophet". In Mark, Herodias would have killed him but could not, "For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy", and "heard him gladly".

Mark tells the feast most fully. On his birthday Herod made a supper for his lords, high captains and chief estates of Galilee; the daughter of Herodias danced and pleased him, and he swore to give her whatever she asked, "unto the half of my kingdom". Told by her mother, she asked for "the head of John the Baptist" in a charger. "The king was exceeding sorry; yet for his oath's sake, and for their sakes which sat with him", he would not refuse her, and he sent an executioner, who beheaded John in the prison. Matthew tells it more briefly: the king "was sorry", but "commanded it to be given her".

Matthew and Mark tell how, hearing of Jesus' fame, Herod said that John the Baptist was risen from the dead; in Mark he says, "It is John, whom I beheaded: he is risen from the dead." In Luke, Herod was perplexed, because some said John had risen. He said, "John have I beheaded: but who is this, of whom I hear such things?" "And he desired to see him."

Three more verses name only Herod, and the site takes them as this man from their setting. Some Pharisees warned Jesus, "Herod will kill thee", and Jesus answered, "Go ye, and tell that fox, Behold, I cast out devils, and I do cures to day and to morrow". Jesus told his disciples to beware "of the leaven of Herod". Among the women who ministered to Jesus was "Joanna the wife of Chuza Herod's steward".

Only Luke tells how, learning that Jesus was a Galilean and so belonged "unto Herod's jurisdiction", Pilate sent him to Herod, who was in Jerusalem at the time. Herod "was exceeding glad" and "hoped to have seen some miracle done by him"; he questioned him "in many words; but he answered him nothing." Herod and his men of war "set him at nought, and mocked him, and arrayed him in a gorgeous robe, and sent him again to Pilate." That day "Pilate and Herod were made friends together". Later, in Jerusalem, the company of Peter and John named "Herod" with Pilate in their prayer, among those gathered "against thy holy child Jesus"; Acts does not say which Herod, and the site takes him as this man.

philip-luk-3-1.short: Brother of Herod the tetrarch, named once in Scripture as tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis in the year John the Baptist began to preach.

paragraphs.text: Philip is named in a single verse. Luke dates the coming of the word of God to John in the wilderness by the rulers of the day, among them "his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis", the brother of Herod the tetrarch of Galilee. Scripture records no word or deed of his, and no meeting with Jesus.

Matthew and Mark name a "Philip", Herod's brother, whose wife Herodias had been. Scripture does not say whether he was this tetrarch. The site keeps them as two people, for reasons set out on this Philip's page as a ruler, along with what is known of him from outside the Bible.

herod-act-12-1.short: The king Acts calls Herod, who killed James the brother of John, imprisoned Peter, and died at Caesarea, smitten by the angel of the Lord.

paragraphs.text: Acts calls this king only "Herod the king" and "Herod". It never calls him Agrippa and does not say whose son he was. The site's reasons for taking him as Herod Agrippa I are explained on his page as a ruler.

"Herod the king stretched forth his hands to vex certain of the church. And he killed James the brother of John with the sword." Because he saw that it pleased the Jews, he arrested Peter too, in the days of unleavened bread. He put him in prison under four quaternions of soldiers, "intending after Easter to bring him forth to the people."

The church prayed for Peter without ceasing. On the night before Herod would have brought him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, when the angel of the Lord raised him up; his chains fell off, and he followed the angel out through the iron gate. Coming to himself, Peter said, "the Lord hath sent his angel, and hath delivered me out of the hand of Herod".

In the morning there was "no small stir among the soldiers". When Herod had searched for Peter and not found him, he examined the keepers "and commanded that they should be put to death." Then he went down from Judaea to Caesarea and stayed there.

Herod "was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon". They made a friend of Blastus, "the king's chamberlain", and asked for peace, "because their country was nourished by the king's country." On a set day Herod, "arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them", and the people shouted, "It is the voice of a god, and not of a man." "And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost." Acts goes on: "But the word of God grew and multiplied."

agrippa-act-25-13.short: King Agrippa came with Bernice to greet Festus at Caesarea, heard Paul's defence, and said Paul might have gone free had he not appealed to Caesar.

paragraphs.text: Acts calls him "king Agrippa" and sets him beside Bernice at Caesarea, in the time of the governor Festus. It never calls him Herod, does not say whose son he was, and does not say how Bernice was related to him. These links, and the site's reasons for taking him as Agrippa II, are explained on his page as a ruler.

"King Agrippa and Bernice came unto Caesarea to salute Festus." After many days Festus laid Paul's case before the king: a man "left in bonds by Felix", accused over questions "of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive." Festus added that Paul had appealed "unto the hearing of Augustus". Agrippa said, "I would also hear the man myself."

The next day Agrippa and Bernice came "with great pomp" into the place of hearing, with the chief captains and the principal men of the city, and Paul was brought in. Festus said he had "no certain thing to write unto my lord", and so had brought Paul "specially before thee, O king Agrippa".

Agrippa said to Paul, "Thou art permitted to speak for thyself." Paul said, "I think myself happy" to answer before him, "because I know thee to be expert in all customs and questions which are among the Jews". He told of his life as a Pharisee, of how he had persecuted the saints, of the light and the voice on the road to Damascus, and of his preaching since. When Festus said with a loud voice that he was beside himself, Paul answered that "the king knoweth of these things", for "this thing was not done in a corner."

Paul turned to him: "King Agrippa, believest thou the prophets? I know that thou believest." "Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." The king rose with the governor and Bernice, and going aside they said among themselves, "This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds." Agrippa said to Festus, "This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar."

herodias-mat-14-3.short: Herod the tetrarch's wife, once his brother Philip's wife; Mark says she wanted John the Baptist dead, and she told her daughter to ask for his head.

paragraphs.text: Herodias had been "his brother Philip's wife", and Herod the tetrarch "had married her". In Mark, John the Baptist told Herod, "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife." Luke says John reproved him "for Herodias his brother Philip's wife"; Matthew and Mark say Herod put John in prison "for Herodias' sake". Mark adds, "Herodias had a quarrel against him, and would have killed him; but she could not: For Herod feared John, knowing that he was a just man and an holy".

On Herod's birthday her daughter danced before the guests and pleased him, and he swore to give her whatever she asked. In Mark the girl went out and asked her mother, "What shall I ask?" and Herodias answered, "The head of John the Baptist." Matthew says the daughter was "before instructed of her mother". John was beheaded in the prison, his head was brought in a charger to the girl, "and the damsel gave it to her mother."
Scripture says nothing more of her. It does not name her daughter or her parents; her place in the family is explained on the page of Herod the tetrarch as a ruler.

bernice-act-25-13.short: A woman who came with king Agrippa to Caesarea and sat with him and the governor Festus to hear Paul; Scripture records no word of hers.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names Bernice three times, all in Acts, and always beside king Agrippa. "King Agrippa and Bernice came unto Caesarea to salute Festus." The next day she came with him "with great pomp" into the place of hearing, where Paul was brought before them.
When Paul had spoken, "the king rose up, and the governor, and Bernice, and they that sat with them". Going aside, they said among themselves, "This man doeth nothing worthy of death or of bonds."
Acts records no word of hers and does not say how she was related to Agrippa. What is known of her from outside the Bible is set out on Agrippa's page as a ruler.
